meta.title: Who really said "There is no road too long to the man who advances deliberately and without undue haste"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: La Bruyère really wrote it — in French, in Les Caractères (1688), aphorism 108 of "Des jugements." The familiar English wording has no named translator.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no road too long to the man who advances deliberately and without undue haste'?
meta.ogDescription: The French original is real and precisely locatable in Les Caractères (1688). The popular English rendering is an unsigned translation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1645–1696 · French moralist & satirist, author of Les Caractères
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely La Bruyère’s: it stands as aphorism 108 of “Des jugements” in Les Caractères (1688), and the French sentence can be read there today. What is not pinned down is the English — this familiar wording matches no published translation that could be located, and the reference that prints it ↗ credits no translator.

source.heading: Where the line actually is

docMeta.dd: English wording carries no translator credit; not Van Laun (1885)

source.excerpt: Il n’y a point de chemin trop long à qui marche lentement et sans se presser ; il n’y a point d’avantages trop éloignés à qui s’y prépare par la patience.
trail: The French sentence is exactly where it is said to be — in the chapter “Des jugements” of Les Caractères. Read it in the Flammarion 1880 text on French Wikisource ↗.
This exact English wording is printed beside the French and cited to Les Caractères (1688), “Des jugements,” aphorism 108 — with no translator named — on Wikiquote’s “Patience” page ↗.

The standard Victorian English version reads quite differently. Henri Van Laun’s translation gives aphorism 108 of “Of Opinions” as “No way is too tedious for him who travels slowly and without being in a hurry; no advantages are too remote for those who have patience” — see the full 1885 translation at Project Gutenberg ↗.
No specialist has flagged the line as fake: a site search of Quote Investigator ↗ returns no article on it.
source.excerptNote: Les Caractères, “Des jugements” — the sentence as printed, unnumbered, in the Flammarion 1880 text on French Wikisource, which separates the aphorisms with pilcrows rather than numbering them. The number 108 is the standard numbering, confirmed against Van Laun 1885, “Of Opinions,” §108, where the same preceding aphorism (the hundred-million-years passage) is §107. The circulating English — “There is no road too long to the man who advances deliberately and without undue haste; there are no honours too distant to the man who prepares himself for them with patience” — is a rendering of this sentence, published without a translator’s name.

sourceLink.text: Les Caractères, "Des jugements" on French Wikisource

source.rightsNote: The French text of Les Caractères (1688) is long out of copyright, and Henri Van Laun’s English translation (London: John C. Nimmo, 1885) is public domain in the United States. This particular English wording, though, has no identified translator and no known first publication date — so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it.

author.name: Jean de La Bruyère
author.heading: Jean de La Bruyère
author.metaLine: 1645–1696 · French philosopher & moralist, author of Les Caractères
author.bio: Jean de La Bruyère was a French philosopher and moralist noted for his satire, born 16 August 1645 and dead on 11 May 1696. His one enduring book, Les Caractères, first appeared in 1688 and kept growing — the fourth edition of 1689 added especially heavily — as he went on inserting fresh portraits of his contemporaries. The result is less a treatise than a mosaic of short character sketches and one-line judgements on the manners of his age, of which this sentence is one.

misattribution.heading: The wording, not the author
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a famous name being handed someone else’s line. La Bruyère wrote the sentence. The soft spot is the English it travels in.

items.why: The circulating English matches no published translation that could be located. Henri Van Laun’s 1885 version ↗ renders the same aphorism as “No way is too tedious for him who travels slowly and without being in a hurry.” The reference work that does print the familiar wording, Wikiquote ↗, credits no translator at all.

La Bruyère wrote avantages — advantages, benefits — in the French text ↗, and Van Laun translated it that way. Turning them into “honours” narrows a general claim about patient effort into one about status and preferment. A defensible choice, but not a literal one.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is real and precisely locatable: Les Caractères (1688), “Des jugements,” aphorism 108 — read the French ↗. It is the English, not the attribution, that is unsourced.

context.heading: Why this one is unusual
lead: Most lines pinned to a famous moralist dissolve when you go looking for the page. This one does the opposite. Les Caractères is a numbered book — each chapter is a run of short, separately numbered reflections — so “Des jugements,” no. 108 is a precise address, and the French sits there exactly as advertised, a few lines after La Bruyère’s remark about how slight an experience of six or seven thousand years really is.

The English is the loose part. La Bruyère wrote avantages; the popular version makes them “honours,” and gives “marche lentement et sans se presser” the rather grander “advances deliberately and without undue haste.” It reads well — better, arguably, than the Victorian rendering — but nobody has signed it, which is why this page stops short of calling the quotation verified.
detailsBody: Henri Van Laun’s The “Characters” of Jean de La Bruyère (London: John C. Nimmo, 1885) is the most widely available complete English version and keeps La Bruyère’s own numbering, which is how aphorism 108 can be checked against the French one sentence at a time. It renders the chapter title “Des jugements” as “Of Opinions.”
context.pull: The French is easy to find. The English is the part nobody signed.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's "Patience" page prints the French original and the English wording "There is no road too long to the man who advances deliberately and without undue haste; there are no honours too distant to the man who prepares himself for them with patience," cited to Jean de La Bruyère, Les Caractères (1688), Des jugements, aphorism 108, with no translator named.

The chapter "Des Jugements" of Les Caractères (Flammarion 1880 text) contains the sentence "Il n'y a point de chemin trop long à qui marche lentement et sans se presser ; il n'y a point d'avantages trop éloignés à qui s'y prépare par la patience."
Project Gutenberg ebook 46633 is The "Characters" of Jean de La Bruyère, author La Bruyère (1645-1696), translated by Henri Van Laun (1820-1896).

The Van Laun text renders aphorism 108 of chapter XII, "Of Opinions," as "No way is too tedious for him who travels slowly and without being in a hurry; no advantages are too remote for those who have patience," and its title page reads "newly rendered into English by Henri Van Laun ... London, John C. Nimmo, 1885." A search of the full text finds no occurrence of "road too long" or "undue haste."

Jean de La Bruyère lived 16 August 1645 – 11 May 1696, was a French philosopher and moralist noted for his satire, and his Les Caractères first appeared in 1688, expanded through successive editions with significant additions in the fourth edition (1689).
